questions.title: Fever from influenza reflects elevation of the set point
questions.subject: fnd
questions.question: A patient with influenza has a body temperature of 39 degrees Celsius. What is the precise underlying mechanism of this elevated temperature?

options.A: Markedly decreased sensitivity of central thermoreceptors
options.B: Elevation of the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point
options.C: Complete failure of all normal heat-loss mechanisms
options.D: Markedly increased sensitivity of peripheral cold receptors

explanations.A: Incorrect. Central thermoreceptor sensitivity is not what is described as failing here; the change is in the target the hypothalamus is defending, not in its ability to sense temperature.
explanations.B: Correct. Pyrogens released during influenza infection elevate the hypothalamic set point above its normal value, and the hypothalamus then drives heat-generating and heat-conserving responses until core temperature rises to match this new, higher target — producing the measured 39-degree fever. The hypothalamus is not malfunctioning here; it is correctly defending a new, higher target that pyrogens have set.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Heat-loss mechanisms are not described as completely failing; rather, they are actively suppressed by the hypothalamus because it is now defending a higher set point, a regulated response rather than a mechanical failure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is not increased peripheral cold-receptor sensitivity that produces fever; the hypothalamus behaves as though the body is cold because its internal set point has been raised, independent of peripheral cold sensing.

questions.learning_objective: Explain fever as pyrogen-mediated resetting of the hypothalamic set point upward, and state that the ensuing shivering and vasoconstriction are the normal response to a body temperature that is now below the new set point.
